title: Part 2, Chapter 6
paragraphs: What passed between Don Quixote and his niece and housekeeper; one of the most important chapters in the whole history

While Sancho Panza and his wife, Teresa Cascajo, were carrying on that beside-the-point conversation, Don Quixote’s niece and housekeeper were anything but idle, for a thousand small signs had begun to tell them that their uncle and master meant to slip away from them a third time and go back to what was, in their view, his ill-errant chivalry. They tried every means in their power to talk him out of so unlucky a scheme, but it was all preaching in the desert and hammering on cold iron. Even so, among the many other arguments they pressed on him, the housekeeper said, “Honestly, master, if you will not stay put and keep quiet at home, and give up roaming the mountains and valleys like a soul in torment, hunting for what people say are called adventures—though I call them misfortunes—then I shall have to take my complaint to God and to the king, crying aloud for them to send some remedy.”

To this Don Quixote replied, “What answer God will give to your complaints, housekeeper, I cannot say, nor what his Majesty will answer either. I only know that if I were king, I would refuse to answer the countless foolish petitions presented to him every day; for one of the greatest among the many burdens kings carry is the obligation to listen to everyone and answer everyone, and so I should be sorry for any business of mine to trouble him.”
At that the housekeeper asked, “Tell us, señor—are there no knights at his Majesty’s court?”
“There are,” answered Don Quixote, “and plenty of them; and it is right there should be, to adorn the dignity of the prince and add to the glory of the king’s majesty.”
“Then couldn’t your worship,” she said, “be one of those who serve their king and lord at his court without stirring a single step?”

“Bear in mind, my friend,” said Don Quixote, “that not all knights can be courtiers, nor can all courtiers be knights-errant, nor do they need to be. The world must have all sorts; and though we may all be knights, there is a vast difference between one kind and another. The courtiers, without ever leaving their rooms or crossing the threshold of the court, travel the whole world by looking at a map, and it costs them not a penny, and they suffer neither heat nor cold, hunger nor thirst. But we, the true knights-errant, measure the entire earth with our own feet, exposed to the sun, to the cold, to the open air, to the harshness of the heavens, by day and by night, on foot and on horseback. Nor do we know our enemies only in pictures: we know them in their own real shapes, and at every risk and on every occasion we attack them, paying no attention to the childish points and rules of single combat—whether one man’s lance or sword is shorter than the other’s, whether he carries relics or some hidden charm about him, whether or not the sunlight is to be divided and apportioned between the fighters, and other niceties of that kind observed in formal man-to-man duels, things you know nothing about, but I do. And you must understand, besides, that the true knight-errant, even if he should see ten giants whose heads not only touch the clouds but pierce through them, giants who walk on two tall towers for legs, whose arms are like the masts of mighty ships, whose every eye is like a great mill-wheel and glows hotter than a glass furnace, must not be frightened by them in the slightest. On the contrary, he must charge and fall upon them with a gallant bearing and a fearless heart, and, if he can, conquer and destroy them—even if they wear for armour the shells of a certain fish said to be harder than diamonds, and instead of swords carry keen blades of Damascus steel, or clubs studded with steel spikes, such as I have seen more than once. I say all this, housekeeper, so that you may see the difference between one sort of knight and the other; and it would be well if there were no prince who did not place a higher value on this second—or, to speak more accurately, first—kind of knight, the errant kind; for, as we read in their histories, there have been some among them who were the salvation not just of one kingdom but of many.”

“Ah, señor,” the niece broke in at this point, “remember that everything you are saying about knights-errant is fable and fiction; and their histories, if they have not already been burned, deserve, every one of them, to have a sambenito hung on them, or some other mark to brand them as infamous and as corrupters of decent behaviour.”

“By the God who gives me life,” said Don Quixote, “if you were not my own niece, the daughter of my own sister, I would punish you for the blasphemy you have just uttered in a way the whole world would hear of. What! Can it be that a young chit who can barely manage a dozen lace-bobbins dares to wag her tongue and pass judgment on the histories of knights-errant? What would Señor Amadis say if he heard such a thing? Though he, no doubt, would forgive you, for he was the most humble-hearted and courteous knight of his age, and a great protector of damsels besides. But there are others who might have heard you, and for you it would not have gone so well in that case, for they are not all courteous or well-mannered; some are ill-tempered scoundrels. Nor is everyone who calls himself a gentleman a gentleman in every respect: some are gold, others mere pinchbeck, and they all look like gentlemen, but not all of them can bear the touchstone of truth. There are men of low rank who strain themselves to bursting to pass for gentlemen, and high-born gentlemen who, you would swear, are dying to pass for men of low rank; the former lift themselves up by ambition or by their virtues, the latter drag themselves down by their want of spirit or by their vices; and it takes experience and discernment to tell apart these two kinds of gentlemen, so alike in name and so different in conduct.”

“God help me!” said the niece. “To think you know so much, uncle—enough, if it came to it, to climb into a pulpit and go preaching in the streets—and yet you fall into a delusion so enormous and a folly so obvious as to insist you are vigorous when you are old, strong when you are sickly, able to straighten what is crooked when you yourself are bent with age, and, above all, that you are a caballero when you are no such thing; for though gentlefolk may be caballeros, poor men never are!”

“There is a great deal of truth in what you say, niece,” Don Quixote answered, “and I could tell you things about birth that would astonish you; but, so as not to mix the human with the divine, I will hold my tongue. Listen, my dears—and pay attention to what I am saying—all the lineages in the world can be reduced to four kinds, and they are these: those that had humble beginnings and went on spreading and extending themselves until they reached extraordinary greatness; those that began great and have maintained that greatness, and still keep and uphold the grandeur of their origin; those, again, that began great and have ended in a point like a pyramid, having whittled and shrunk their original greatness down to nothing—like the tip of a pyramid, which, compared with its base or foundation, is nothing at all; and finally those—and they are the most numerous—that had neither an illustrious beginning nor a remarkable middle, and so will come to an end without a name, like any ordinary plebeian line. Of the first kind, those that rose from humble origins to the greatness they still hold, the house of the Ottomans may stand as an example, which from a humble, lowly shepherd, its founder, has climbed to the height at which we now see it. For examples of the second kind of lineage, which began in greatness and preserves it still without adding to it, there are the many princes who have inherited their rank and keep themselves within their inheritance, neither enlarging nor diminishing it, living peacefully inside the borders of their states. Of those that began great and have dwindled to a point, there are thousands of examples: all the Pharaohs and Ptolemies of Egypt, the Caesars of Rome, and the whole herd—if I may use such a word for them—of countless princes, monarchs, and lords, Medes, Assyrians, Persians, Greeks, and barbarians. All these lineages and lordships have ended in a point and come to nothing, they and their founders alike, for it would be impossible today to find a single one of their descendants, and even if we did find one, he would be in some lowly and humble station. Of plebeian lineages I have nothing to say, except that they serve merely to swell the ranks of the living, with no distinction to earn them any fame or praise beyond that. From all I have said, my poor innocents, I want you to gather this: that the confusion among lineages is very great, and that the only ones seen to be great and illustrious are those that prove it by the virtue, the wealth, and the generosity of those who bear them. I say virtue, wealth, and generosity, because a great man who is vicious will be nothing but a great example of vice, and a rich man who is not generous will be merely a miserly beggar; for the owner of wealth is not made happy by owning it but by spending it—and not by spending it however he pleases, but by knowing how to spend it well. The poor gentleman has no way of showing he is a gentleman except by virtue: by being affable, well-bred, courteous, gentle in manner, and kind; not haughty, arrogant, or fault-finding; and above all by being charitable, for with two maravedis given to the poor with a cheerful heart he will show himself as generous as the man who hands out alms to the ringing of bells; and no one who sees him graced with the virtues I have named, even without knowing who he is, will fail to recognise him and set him down as a man of good blood. Indeed it would be strange if it were otherwise: praise has always been the reward of virtue, and the virtuous cannot fail to win commendation. There are two roads, my daughters, by which men may arrive at wealth and honours: one is the road of letters, the other the road of arms. I have more of arms than of letters in my make-up, and, to judge by my bent for arms, I was born under the influence of the planet Mars. I am therefore all but compelled to follow that road, and follow it I must in spite of the whole world; and you will labour in vain trying to persuade me to resist what heaven wills, what fate ordains, what reason demands, and what, above all, my own inclination favours. For knowing as I do the countless hardships that go hand in hand with knight-errantry, I know too the infinite blessings that are won by it. I know that the path of virtue is very narrow and the road of vice broad and spacious; I know their ends and destinations are different, for the broad, easy road of vice ends in death, and the narrow, toilsome path of virtue ends in life—not life that passes away, but life that has no end. I know, as our great Castilian poet says, that—

It is by rugged paths like these men climb
Toward the high seat of immortality,
Never attained by those who falter below.”

“Oh, misery!” cried the niece. “My lord is a poet as well! He knows everything; he can do everything. I would wager that if he took it into his head to turn mason, he could build a house as easily as a birdcage.”

“I can promise you, niece,” Don Quixote replied, “that if these thoughts of chivalry did not claim every faculty I have, there would be nothing I could not do, no piece of handiwork that would not come from these hands of mine—particularly cages and toothpicks.”

Just then there came a knocking at the door, and when they asked who was there, Sancho Panza answered that it was he. The moment the housekeeper realised who it was, she ran off to hide so as not to have to look at him—such was her loathing for the man. The niece let him in, and his master Don Quixote came forward to welcome him with open arms, and the two shut themselves up in his room, where they held another conversation in no way inferior to the last.
